messages.subject: Strange scale_x_datetime offset?
messages.body_plain:
I often plot data from a data frame that has both a POSIXct and a
numeric column.  The following code creates such a data frame and plots
the data:

require(ggplot2)
require(scales)
require(lubridate)
timelist <- ymd_hm(c("2013-05-01 12:00","2013-05-02 18:00","2013-05-03 06:00"),tz="America/Los_Angeles")
sampleDF <- data.frame(time = timelist, values = c(3,4,2))
qplot(time, values, data = sampleDF)+scale_x_datetime(minor_breaks=date_breaks("6 hour"))

When I run the code above, I get a plot with the three points at the
right times, but the minor break lines are offset apparently by 3 hours
from the axis.  I expected the minor breaks to coincide with the major
breaks.  That is, I expected minor breaks at 0:00, 6:00, 12:00, 18:00,
..., with major breaks as scales chose, but I get minor breaks at 3:00,
9:00, ....

My time zone is "America/Los_Angeles", but I get the same result when I
use "UTC" for the data instead.

What can I do to get what I expected?  What controls where the minor
breaks start?

Thanks,

Bill
--
Bill Harris
Facilitated Systems
http://makingsense.facilitatedsystems.com/

messages.subject: Re: problem of line proportionality
messages.body_plain:
I'm sorry but I have to insist with my proportionality problem. With geom_line() or geom_segment() (see example before), I sometimes get a better proportionality adding scale_size(), but it's not accurate and I can't understand why. I mean, when I set a colour I get exactly that colour, when I set a position I get exactly that position, but when I set a proportion I just get nearly (if lucky) that proportion.

Please try this, there is a factor 2 difference in the value, but a factor 6 difference in the proportion :

xori <- c(1, 2)
xend <- c(2, 3)
yori <- c(2, 4)
yend <- c(1, 2)
val <- c(10, 20)
df <- data.frame(xori, xend, yori, yend, val)

ggplot(df) + geom_segment(aes(x = xori, y = yori, xend = xend, yend = yend, size = val))

Please help !

--
Hadrien

messages.subject: Re: Strange scale_x_datetime offset? [SCL:5]
messages.body_plain:
I've been following the conversation and was able to reproduce the issue Bill described. The first solution proposed also failed to solve the problem for me. I'm not sure the second solution quite works either.

To consolidate the discussion and make comparison easy, I'm reporting the three code variations below and attaching PNGs of each graph they code produced. I comment on how each piece of code behaved for me and then I add some additional thoughts and attempts at producing the behavior Bill seems to be going for. (Note: I double checked that my R and packages were all updated. My timezone is PST.)

Here's the data setup code (as provided by Bill):

require(ggplot2)
require(scales)
require(lubridate)
timelist <- ymd_hm(c("2013-05-01 12:00","2013-05-02 18:00","2013-05-03 06:00"),tz="America/Los_Angeles")
sampleDF <- data.frame(time = timelist, values = c(3,4,2))

> sampleDF
                 time values
1 2013-05-01 12:00:00      3
2 2013-05-02 18:00:00      4
3 2013-05-03 06:00:00      2

Here's the first plot code (as provided by Bill):

qplot(time, values, data = sampleDF)+scale_x_datetime(minor_breaks=date_breaks("6 hour"))

- on my computer: major/minor breaks are oddly aligned so that minor breaks don't nicely parse the space between the major breaks - this makes the spacing look "uneven" (similar to Bill to I think)

Here's the first solution proposed (as provided by Hadri):

qplot(time, values, data = sampleDF) + scale_x_datetime(limits = c(min(timelist), max(timelist)), minor_breaks=date_breaks("6 hour"))

- on my computer: major/minor breaks are still oddly aligned and space still looks uneven (similar to Bill I think). in fact, I see no changes from the graph produced by the original code.

Here's the second solution proposed (as provided by Hadri):

qplot(time, values, data = sampleDF)+scale_x_datetime(breaks=date_breaks("6 hour"), minor_breaks = date_breaks("3 hour"))

- on my computer: the space is now evenly parsed but the major breaks seem oddly placed (on 21, 3, 9, ... instead of 0, 6, 12, ...).

Even though this solution works, I'm still confused as to why the breaks lined up so oddly in the first place. I suspect this solution simply masks the mis-alignment going on between the major/minor breaks by having the minor breaks "overfill."

For instance, I think Bill wanted this:
major minor
0            0

              6

12        12

But got this:
major minor
0
             3

             9
12

The current solution gives this:
major minor
              0
3            3
              6
9            9
             12

The mis-alignment is still there - we've just masked it by having the minor breaks fill in the gaps.

In fact, reading through ??scale_x_datetime, I am confused why the following doesn't work to give the behavior Bill seems to want.

third solution (using the default minor breaks)

qplot(time, values, data = sampleDF)+scale_x_datetime(breaks=date_breaks("12 hour"))

The major breaks occur every 12 hours with a minor break marked in between each (the default behavior when minor breaks aren't specified) at the 6 hour marks. This is the correct spacing and has removed the major/minor misalignment. However, now the grid lines up poorly with the data and (at least to me) the breaks seem illogical since they are at odd times (21, 3, 9, ...).

I think this is what Hadri's first solution was attempting to address - by adjusting the start/end points of the scale to the min/max values, we should get better aligned breaks. Yet this doesn't work as anticipated - it doesn't change my graph at all. I think the graph already assigned these values as default.

Perhaps it's the "expand" feature of scale_x_datetime? This feature seems to put space between the min/max values on the scale and the edges of the drawn grid. I wasn't able to figure out how to make "expand" work directly, but I was able to "force" the data into the desired alignment by adjusting the values in "limits".

fourth solution (shifting the scale minimum to line up the first time with a major break)

qplot(time, values, data = sampleDF)+scale_x_datetime(breaks=date_breaks("12 hour"), limits = c(as.POSIXct("2013-05-01 3:00:00 PDT"), as.POSIXct("2013-05-03 08:00:00 PDT")))

The main problem with this "solution" is that it draws too much of the range before the first data-point... =/

I still suspect that "expand" might be the place to look for an alignment solution...

And that's where I stopped for the day. =)

Warm regards,
Brian

messages.body_plain:
Hi Adam:

Here's a revision of Baptiste's function in the old theming system to
work in the new one, using an example from one of his posts on the
topic.

# The title as a text string:
title <- "Marker 1: Similar to AAA80501.1 Lycopersicon esculentum;
unknown; Solanum lycopersicum unknown oxidase-like protein mRNA,
complete cds; similar to hyoscyamine 6beta-hydroxylase: SwissProt
Accession Number P24397, flavavone-3-hydroxylase: PIR Accession Number
S36233, and ethylene forming enzyme: encoded by GenBank Accession
number M90294 ;cl209ct403cn544 ;COMPLETE ;RESISTANCE(6), FLOWER(71),
FRUIT(7)"

# The function to process the string

splitString <- function (text, width)
{
  if(is.null(text)) return(NULL)
  strings <- strsplit(text, " ")[[1]]
  newstring <- strings[1]
  linewidth <- stringWidth(newstring)
  gapwidth <- stringWidth(" ")
  availwidth <- convertWidth(width, "inches", valueOnly = TRUE)
  for (i in 2:length(strings)) {
    width <- stringWidth(strings[i])
        if (convertWidth(linewidth + gapwidth + width, "inches",
            valueOnly = TRUE) < availwidth) {
            sep <- " "
            linewidth <- linewidth + gapwidth + width
        }
        else {
            sep <- "\n"
            linewidth <- width
        }
        newstring <- paste(newstring, strings[i], sep = sep)
    }
  newstring
}

# Application of the function
newtitle <- splitString(title, unit(10, "cm"))
qplot(1:10, 1:10) + ggtitle(newtitle)

Dennis

Hi Adam,

plotmath support seems a bit inconsistent in ggplot2, requiring
different methods for different plot elements. I can see some sense in
it (e.g., for geoms you would expect the values to be strings not
expressions, so having a way to convert them makes sense; for plot and
axis titles we can easily construct the expressions ourselves).
Nonetheless, the overall effect is that it seems like a hodgepodge of
methods have to be used depending on what one is trying to do.

Fortunately it is all spelled out for us at
https://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/wiki/Plotmath. For your example you
are just missing the fact that arguments to expression should be
unquoted:

ggplot(cars,aes(speed,dist))+geom_point()+
        geom_smooth()+
        labs(title=expression(paste(rho==0.081)))+ # works

        annotate("text",x=1,y=120,label=paste("rho==0.081"),parse=T) #works

Best,
Ista

>          labs(title=expression(paste("rho==0.081")))+ #does not work
>          annotate("text",x=1,y=120,label=paste("rho==0.081"),parse=T)
> #works

For the title you want

     labs(title=expression(rho==0.081))

In the annotation, it is expressed as a string which is then to be
parsed as an expression (what parse=TRUE does). But in a direct
expression, quoted material is literal strings and is not further parsed.

This should get you back to your original problem.

messages.subject: Re: Strange scale_x_datetime offset? [SCL:5]
messages.body_plain:
Alright. I /think/ I've arrived at a pair of working solutions and maybe a better sense of why Bill's data graph oddly.

Here's my logic:
1. The grid breaks seem to be dependent on (or influenced by) the scale minimum. So, for instance, if we happen to have a minimum that is "odd", then we seem to get odd breaks.
2. The scale minimum seems to be influenced both by the "limits" argument and the "expand" argument. "limits" says what the minimum should be and "expand" shapes how far the edge of the graph should be from the minimum.
3. The default setting of "expand" may make time scales behave in unexpected ways. scale_x_datetime seems to derive a lot of its behavior from scale_x_continuous. Continuous scales, however, tend to either be anchored at 0 (which would make for predictable break behavior) or are non-cyclical (perhaps making odd breaks less obvious).

If this idea is correct, then Bill's graph looks odd because the "expand" default values are shifting the starting point of the drawn grid. This shift, in turn, is shifting the x-axis breaks off of the minimum data value. This produces illogical breaks since we're working with cyclical, time-incremented data.

We should be able to force the breaks the line up with our time data in two ways.

First, we could set the "expand" argument so that it does nothing - this should force the grid to start at our "limits" minimum. We could either let this be the minimum value in our data (though will partially occlude this point) or pick a minimum that we find reasonable.

creating the example data (from Bill's original post)

require(ggplot2)
require(scales)
require(lubridate)
timelist <- ymd_hm(c("2013-05-01 12:00","2013-05-02 18:00","2013-05-03 06:00"),tz="America/Los_Angeles")
sampleDF <- data.frame(time = timelist, values = c(3,4,2))

working solution 1: removing the "expand" effect and forcing a desirable start value (see attached PNG)
p <- ggplot(sampleDF, aes(x = time, y = values))
p + geom_point() + scale_x_datetime(breaks = date_breaks("12 hour"), limits = c(as.POSIXct("2013-05-01 0:00:00 PDT"), as.POSIXct("2013-05-03 24:00:00 PDT")), expand = c(0, 0))

* NOTE: I switched to ggplot rather than the qplot syntax to help me think this through.

Second, we could give an exact list of our major breaks rather than simply specifying the interval. This should circumvent the default behaviors that are setting odd breaks.

working solution 2: specifying all major breaks explicitly (see attached PNG)
# create desired timelist (sorry this is a REALLY inefficient way of doing this - I think the chron package would handle this better)
startTime <- as.POSIXct("2013-05-01 0:00:00 PDT")
majorBreak <- as.duration(interval(start = as.POSIXct("2013-05-01 0:00:00 PDT"), end = as.POSIXct("2013-05-01 12:00:00 PDT")))
increments <- (3 * 24) / 12 # days in range * hours, divide the result by the break interval

majorBreakSet <- c(startTime)
for(i in (1:increments)) {
  newTime <- majorBreakSet[1] + (majorBreak * i)
  majorBreakSet <- c(majorBreakSet, newTime)
}

# now create the graph with the explicit major breaks - go ahead and allow default minor break and expand behavior, should work fine
p <- ggplot(sampleDF, aes(x = time, y = values))
p + geom_point() + scale_x_datetime(breaks = majorBreakSet)

This solution let's us make use of the default ggplot behaviors. This is especially nice because it ignores some of the sillier explicit breaks I set (the start and end breaks) which fall kinda far from our data. We could, however, force it to respect these breaks by adjusting "limits" if we wanted and still have things nicely lined up the way we intended.

I hope this helps and thanks for the fun discussion!!

Warm regards,
Brian

Hi Adam,

plotmath support seems a bit inconsistent in ggplot2, requiring
different methods for different plot elements. I can see some sense in
it (e.g., for geoms you would expect the values to be strings not
expressions, so having a way to convert them makes sense; for plot and
axis titles we can easily construct the expressions ourselves).

methods have to be used depending on what one is trying to do.

Fortunately it is all spelled out for us at
https://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/wiki/Plotmath. For your example you
are just missing the fact that arguments to expression should be
unquoted:

ggplot(cars,aes(speed,dist))+geom_point()+
       geom_smooth()+
       labs(title=expression(paste(rho==0.081)))+ # works
       annotate("text",x=1,y=120,label=paste("rho==0.081"),parse=T) #works

Best,
Ista

I agree with the other respondents regarding the distinguishability of
color differences when you have a palette with a large number of
colors, but if you insist, you could look into the colorRampPalette()
function, several of the predefined palette functions (e.g.,
rainbow(), topo.colors(), terrain.colors()) and the colorspace
package...and then confirm the warning :)

Here is a toy example for illustration:

library(ggplot2)
qplot(LETTERS[1:5], geom = "bar", fill = LETTERS[1:5]) +
    coord_polar() + scale_fill_manual(values = rainbow(5))

qplot(LETTERS[1:25], geom = "bar", fill = LETTERS[1:25]) +
    coord_polar() + scale_fill_manual(values = rainbow(25))

# Same idea, different palette
qplot(LETTERS[1:25], geom = "bar", fill = LETTERS[1:25]) +
    coord_polar() +
    scale_fill_manual(values = colorRampPalette(c("navy", "yellow"))(25))

Dennis

messages.body_plain:
Hey Stephen,

If I'm following your intention, I think your solution doesn't require an additional layer or adjustment (e.g., adding scale_colour_manual to the mix). For the smoothing geom (smooth_geom), you can instead map the color aesthetic to hlv just like you mapped the group aesthetic to hlv. You mapped groups to hlv - this will shape how many geoms are produced (one for each group). Now you just need to map color the same way (assigning one color for each group).

Here's the code I used:
ggplot(preemlong, aes(x = event, y = SCORE, group = id)) + geom_smooth(aes(group = hlv, color = hlv), se = F, size = 2)

A PNG of the graph this produced is attached.

Your code is just about there... Just need to add one more argument to the geom_smooth aesthetic set.

Warm regards,
Brian

messages.body_plain:
Hi Antonio,

Here is one way (maybe not the best way, and not checked to make sure
it actually gives the right result...):

library(ggplot2)

avg.w <- read.csv("~/Downloads/avg.country.csv")

library(plyr)

avg.c <- ddply(avg.w, "country", function(DF) { # for each country
    # get the start index
    start <- c(1, which(diff(as.numeric(DF$democracy)) !=0))
    # get the end index
    l <- rle(as.character(DF$democracy))
    end <- cumsum(l$lengths)
    # return a data.frame of:
    data.frame(democracy = l$values, #democracy
               start=DF[start, "birth_year"], #start year
               end=DF[end, "birth_year"] #end year
               )
})

## plot
p1 <- ggplot(data=avg.w)+
    geom_rect(aes(xmin=start,
                  xmax=end,
                  ymin=-Inf,
                  ymax=Inf,
                  fill=democracy, alpha=.4),
              data=avg.c) +
    geom_point(aes(x=birth_year,
                   y=mean,
                   group=wealth2,
                   color=wealth2)) +
    geom_smooth(aes(x=birth_year,
                    y=mean,
                    group=wealth2,
                    color=wealth2)) +
    facet_wrap(~country)

Best,

messages.subject: Re: Palette with more colours
messages.body_plain:
Just to add one more nuance to Dennis's example: Despite the difficulty of distinguishing small differences between large numbers of colors, if you're set on using a large number, adding a third color to the colorRampPalette function might make the colors a bit more distinguishable, though perhaps harder to interpret if the categories are ordered. For example, in Dennis's example, you could do "values=colorRampPalette(c("red", "navy", "yellow"))(25))". This will give you 25 colors that ramp from red to blue and then from blue to yellow.

Joel

On Thursday, June 6, 2013 11:54:54 AM UTC-7, Dennis Murphy wrote:
> I agree with the other respondents regarding the distinguishability of
> color differences when you have a palette with a large number of
> colors, but if you insist, you could look into the colorRampPalette()
> function, several of the predefined palette functions (e.g.,
> rainbow(), topo.colors(), terrain.colors()) and the colorspace
> package...and then confirm the warning :)

> Here is a toy example for illustration:
>
> library(ggplot2)
> qplot(LETTERS[1:5], geom = "bar", fill = LETTERS[1:5]) +
>     coord_polar() + scale_fill_manual(values = rainbow(5))
>
> qplot(LETTERS[1:25], geom = "bar", fill = LETTERS[1:25]) +
>     coord_polar() + scale_fill_manual(values = rainbow(25))
>
> # Same idea, different palette
> qplot(LETTERS[1:25], geom = "bar", fill = LETTERS[1:25]) +

messages.subject: Re: Strange scale_x_datetime offset? [SCL:5]
messages.body_plain:
"Brian \"Meyer\" Waismeyer" <meye...@gmail.com> writes:

> We should be able to force the breaks the line up with our time data in two
> ways.

Thanks, Brian.  You've done a lot on this.  Hadri has, too, but the
solutions don't work as well for me.  That said, these don't seem ideal,
either.

> First, we could set the "expand" argument so that it does nothing - this
> should force the grid to start at our "limits" minimum. We could either let
> this be the minimum value in our data (though will partially occlude this
> point) or pick a minimum that we find reasonable.

This seems to work.  I can simulate the expand option (which I had never
used) artificially by subtracting and adding time to the limits.

Still, the code begins to become baroque, with setting expand and limits
and then rounding and offsetting limits to simulate the effect I wanted
originally.

> *working solution 2: specifying all major breaks explicitly (see attached
> PNG)*

If the first solution is baroque, this seems rococco: to work with
varied data sets, I have to calculate the breaks explicitly from
whatever data I use.

Neither seem consistent with the general way other scales that I've used
work.  It seems quite arcane and undocumented compared to most of
ggplot2.  I'll probably use the first, submit a documentation request to
explain it, and hope it turns into a change in ggplot2.

Thanks to both of you for engaging with this.  I've learned a few
things.

Bill

p <- ggplot( ... )

print( p + theme(legend.position="none") )

Ben

messages.subject: Re: facet_grid not compatible with error bars?
messages.subject_clean: facet_grid not compatible with error bars?
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

The data has to be re-sorted to for the facets, so your points and
errorbars are no longer matching. Omit the reference to the data frame
in your geom_errorbarh call and all should be well:

ggplot(cdata, aes(y=Depth, x = av, shape = TR1, color = TR1))   +
  geom_point(size = 1) +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmax = av+se, xmin =  av-se)) +
  facet_grid(Station~Code)

Best,
Ista

messages.subject: Creating functions that use ggplot
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Considering the following example:

set.seed(1)
mat <- matrix(rnorm(100), nc=5)
rownames(mat) <- letters[1:20]
colnames(mat) <- LETTERS[1:5]

library(ggplot2)
library(reshape2)
toPlot <- melt(mat)

myf <- function(input){
    myp <- ggplot(input, aes(x=Var1, y=Var2, fill=value))
    myp <- myp + geom_tile(colour='white')
    myp <- myp + scale_fill_gradient(low='white', high='steelblue')
    myp
}

myf(toPlot)

what's the best strategy to generalize myf() just so that aesthetics
'x', 'y' and 'fill' are not hard-coded (to Var1, Var2 and value,
respectively)?

I was hoping that something like:

myg <- function(input, xi, yi, zi){
    myp <- ggplot(input, aes(x=as.name <http://as.name>(xi), y=as.name <http://as.name>(yi), fill=as.name <http://as.name>(zi)))
    myp <- myp + geom_tile(colour='white')
    myp <- myp + scale_fill_gradient(low='white', high='steelblue')
    myp
}

would work, but I'm obviously missing something important...

Any thoughts on how to proceed?

Thanks a million,
benilton

On 6/13/2013 11:01 PM, Malcolm Cook wrote:
> I have a custom labeller that recodes logical() as character()['N','Y']
> defined as
>
> YN_labeller<-function(var,val) if(is.logical(val)) {ifelse(val,'Y','N')}
> else label_value(var,val)
>
> It works fine to relabel all my logicals as 'Y' 'N'.
>
> However, when I ALSO pass `margins=TRUE` I get error:  invalid to change
> the storage mode of a factor
>
>
>
> All workarounds happily received, especially if the accomplish the same
> effect by different means.
>
> Cheers
>
> ~Malcolm

I don't see the error you are seeing. Here is a reproducible example:

library("ggplot2")

mtc <- transform(mtcars, lowcarb = carb < 3.5)

p <- ggplot(mtc, aes(wt, mpg)) + geom_point()

YN_labeller <- function(var,val) {

   if(is.logical(val)) {
     ifelse(val,'Y','N')
   } else {
     label_value(var,val)
   }
}

p + facet_grid(~lowcarb)
p + facet_grid(~lowcarb, labeller=YN_labeller)
p + facet_grid(~lowcarb, labeller=YN_labeller, margins=TRUE)

All three plots at the end plot and non give an error. The last one does
not convert FALSE and TRUE to N and Y, but it doesn't give an error. To
understand why no conversion is done for the last one with margins, it
helps to add a `str(var)` and `str(val)` to the beginning of
`YN_labeller`. With that addition you get, for the last two plots:

 > p + facet_grid(~lowcarb, labeller=YN_labeller)
  chr "lowcarb"
  logi [1:2] FALSE TRUE
 > p + facet_grid(~lowcarb, labeller=YN_labeller, margins=TRUE)
  chr "lowcarb"
  Factor w/ 3 levels "FALSE","TRUE",..: 1 2 3

You see, when there is a margin, the values (`val`) have been promoted
to a character and then factor, with "(all)" added as a possible level.
So the `val`'s aren't logical anymore (which they could not be since
there is an "(all)" option).

Here is a version of `YN_labeller` which (also) doesn't throw an error
and does convert the TRUE/FALSE into Y/N even when there is a margin:

YN_labeller <- function(var,val) {

   if(is.logical(val)) {
     ifelse(val,'Y','N')

   } else {
     label <- label_value(var,val)
     label[label=="FALSE"] <- "N"
     label[label=="TRUE"] <- "Y"
     label
   }
}

--
Brian S. Diggs, PhD
Senior Research Associate, Department of Surgery
Oregon Health & Science University

Hi:

First of all, when you post data to an R-related group in an e-mail, please post it in dput() form - it is a text format that retains the original structure of your data.  Tab-delimited copy-and-paste is not recommended - this is especially true of Excel data. Below, I called your data frame DF, and this is how you would produce its dput form, where the Date variable has been converted to Date format, the Site variable to factor and SamplingVariability is left as character:

> dput(DF)
structure(list(Site = structure(c(1L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 1L,
1L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 2L, 2L, 2L,
2L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 2L,
2L), .Label = c("A", "B"), class = "factor"), Date = structure(c(12784,
12785, 12786, 12787, 12788, 12789, 12790, 12791, 12792, 12793,
12794, 12795, 12796, 12797, 12798, 12799, 12800, 12801, 12802,
12803, 12784, 12785, 12786, 12787, 12788, 12789, 12790, 12791,
12792, 12793, 12794, 12795, 12796, 12797, 12798, 12799, 12800,
12801, 12802, 12803), class = "Date"), Value = c(3L, 2L, 4L,
3L, 4L, 5L, 2L, 8L, 6L, 4L, 8L, 6L, 7L, 4L, 8L, 3L, 9L, 2L, 4L,
1L, 10L, 12L, 3L, 4L, 9L, 10L, 10L, 14L, 9L, 8L, 15L, 12L, 9L,
13L, 10L, 8L, 8L, 11L, 12L, 8L), SamplingValidity = c("Valid",
"Valid", "Valid", "Invalid", "Invalid", "Invalid", "Invalid",
"Valid", "Valid", "Valid", "Valid", "Valid", "Valid", "Invalid",
"Invalid", "Invalid", "Valid", "Valid", "Valid", "Valid", "Invalid",
"Invalid", "Invalid", "Valid", "Valid", "Valid", "Valid", "Invalid",
"Invalid", "Invalid", "Invalid", "Valid", "Valid", "Valid", "Valid",
"Valid", "Valid", "Valid", "Valid", "Valid")), .Names = c("Site",
"Date", "Value", "SamplingValidity"), row.names = c(NA, -40L), class = "data.frame")

If the data frame is too large, save it to a file and post a link - one can use the dget() function to read it into R. When you post data in this form, all someone has to do is type

DF <- <copy-paste starting from structure...>

Having said that, here's one way to get what you want, although it uses at least one sleazy trick. As Ben noted, you need to create an external data frame for the start-end dates delimiting the Valid/Invalid periods - there's no way around that.

library(ggplot2)

# The purpose of this chunk is to find the locations of the
# begin and end dates of each Valid/Invalid period
s <- rle(DF$SamplingValidity)
beginDates <- cumsum(c(1, s$lengths[-length(s$lengths)]))
endDates <- cumsum(s$lengths)

# Select out the records corresponding to the border dates;
# the Value variable is excised and the end dates are
# appended as a new variable.
periods <- DF[beginDates, -3]
names(periods)[2] <- "startDate"
periods$endDate <- DF[endDates, "Date"]
str(periods)
periods

# The sleazy trick is to subtract 0.5 from the start dates and
# add 0.5 to the end dates to avoid color gaps between periods.
# I tried this out as a lark and it worked, so left it in. This works
# because, when plotted, dates are converted to a numeric value
# relative to its time origin (default 1970-01-01). A more
# elegant solution would be to use something like the lubridate
# package to get actual date-times for borders. I prefer this
# approach because all points plotted within a period are inside
# a rectangle rather than on a border.
ggplot() +
   theme_bw() +
   geom_rect(data = periods,
             aes(xmin = startDate - 0.5, xmax = endDate + 0.5,
                 ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf,
                 fill = SamplingValidity),
             alpha = 0.2) +
   geom_line(data = DF, aes(x = Date, y = Value), size = 1) +
   scale_fill_manual(values = c("red", "blue")) +
   facet_wrap( ~ Site)

Notice that the externally created data frame periods is used to generate the background rectangles while the original data is used to produce the line plots. You can use scale_x_date() to change features associated with the date scale; see the scales package for details.

Dennis

messages.subject: stat_smooth with method = "gamlss"
messages.body_plain:
Dear forumists,

My apologies if this has been addressed before.

The following will illustrate the problem with pseudo data. I am using R 3.0.1.

library(ggplot2)
library(gamlss)
 r1=rnorm(100)
 r2=rnorm(100)
 d=data.frame(r1,r2)

p=ggplot(d,aes(r1,r2))+geom_point()+stat_smooth(method="gamlss", formula=y~x,family=NO,se=F)

print(p)
GAMLSS-RS iteration 1: Global Deviance = 274.2988
GAMLSS-RS iteration 2: Global Deviance = 274.2988
Error in data.frame(data, source = namelist) :
  arguments imply differing number of rows: 80, 81

The gamlss package is fine in this case as this will show

mod1 = gamlss(formula=r2~r1,family=NO,data=d)

GAMLSS-RS iteration 1: Global Deviance = 274.2988
GAMLSS-RS iteration 2: Global Deviance = 274.2988

summary(mod1)  yields the model estimate as expected

What do I need to do to get stat_smooth to work with the gamlss method?

Daniel

messages.subject: multiple lines plots with different colours
messages.subject_clean: multiple lines plots with different colours
messages.body_plain:
Dear ggplotters,

I am trying to do a very simple graph but for some reason I get a very messy plot.

My dataset is DFsel where I plot y=year and x=value for the variable age_TFR that has two values 1 and 2. What I want to obtain is two lines of two different colours for all the provinces in the plot (defines in prove_geo), except for a single province that I want to highlight with different colours (Barcelona prov_num=38). When I plot by geo_points there is no problem, but since I want lines the following code gives me a messy vertical lines plot.
Also, how can I plot Barcelona with a different colour of my choice?

p <- ggplot(DFsel, aes(year,value, colour=age_TFR))
p + geom_line() +
   labs(title = "Total Period Fertility Rate: Age contribution to total fertility",
        x = "", y = "") +
theme(axis.text     = element_text(colour="grey", size=8, angle=0,
                                      face = "plain"),
         axis.text.x  = element_text(hjust=.5, vjust=.7),
         axis.text.y  = element_text(hjust=1, vjust=0),
         strip.text.x  = element_text(size = 8, colour =
                                        "black", angle = 0),
         plot.title      = element_text(size=20),
         plot.margin = unit(c(1,1,1,1), "cm")
                            ) +

  facet_wrap(~ prov_geo, ncol=6)

I appreciate any help on the matter.

Ale

messages.subject: Plotting Histograms and a Logistic Curve on the Same Plot
messages.subject_clean: Plotting Histograms and a Logistic Curve on the Same Plot
messages.body_plain:
The function loghistplot at http://schamberlain.github.io/2012/01/logistic-regression-barplot-fig/ is supposed to plot a logistic regression curve and, instead of plotting points, it plots a histogram for the 0's and a histogram for the 1's. It looks like he created 3 plots and somehow superimposed them on top of each other using viewports. I recently tried running it again and it was not working. Does anyone know what is wrong or a different way to achieve the same plot? I do not know anything about the grid package. Thanks.

Here is the code with more up to date ggplot2 syntax.

loghistplot <- function(data) {

  require(ggplot2); require(gridExtra) # load packages

  names(data) <- c('x','y') # rename columns

  # get min and max axis values
  min_x <- min(data$x)
  max_x <- max(data$x)
  min_y <- min(data$y)
  max_y <- max(data$y)

  # get bin numbers
  bin_no <- max(hist(data$x)$counts) + 5

  # create plots
  a <- ggplot(data, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
    theme_bw(base_size=16) +
    geom_smooth(method = "glm", family = "binomial", se = TRUE,
                colour='black', size=1.5, alpha = 0.3) +
    # scale_y_continuous(limits=c(0,1), breaks=c(0,1)) +
    scale_x_continuous(limits=c(min_x,max_x)) +
    theme(panel.grid.major = element_blank(),
         panel.grid.minor=element_blank(),
         panel.background = element_blank()) +
    labs(y = "Probability\n", x = "\nYour X Variable")

  b <- ggplot(data[data$y == unique(data$y)[1], ], aes(x = x)) +
    theme_bw(base_size=16) +
    geom_histogram(fill = "grey") +
    scale_y_continuous(limits=c(0,bin_no)) +
    scale_x_continuous(limits=c(min_x,max_x)) +
    theme(panel.grid.major = element_blank(),
         panel.grid.minor=element_blank(),
         axis.text.y = element_blank(),
         axis.text.x = element_blank(),
         axis.ticks = element_blank(),
         panel.border = element_blank(),
         panel.background = element_blank()) +
    labs(y='\n', x='\n')

  c <- ggplot(data[data$y == unique(data$y)[2], ], aes(x = x)) +
    theme_bw(base_size=16) +
    geom_histogram(fill = "grey") +
    scale_y_continuous(trans='reverse', limits=c(bin_no,0)) +
    scale_x_continuous(limits=c(min_x,max_x)) +
    theme(panel.grid.major = element_blank(),panel.grid.minor=element_blank(),
         axis.text.y = element_blank(), axis.text.x = element_blank(),
         axis.ticks = element_blank(),
         panel.border = element_blank(),
         panel.background = element_blank()) +
    labs(y='\n', x='\n')

  grid.newpage()
  pushViewport(viewport(layout = grid.layout(1,1)))

  vpa_ <- viewport(width = 1, height = 1, x = 0.5, y = 0.5)
  vpb_ <- viewport(width = 1, height = 1, x = 0.5, y = 0.5)
  vpc_ <- viewport(width = 1, height = 1, x = 0.5, y = 0.5)

  print(b, vp = vpb_)
  print(c, vp = vpc_)
  print(a, vp = vpa_)
}
loghistplot(mtcars[,c("mpg","vs")])

2) The thing below the red line (I will call it the ALPHA TERM): I would prefer an alpha (greek letter with * after the letter) exactly positioned at the y-axis. It should belong to the legend.

3) How can I reduce the decimal places if I use geom_text?

4) I would like to move the label ("rs...") (see LABEL TERM) slightly to the right. Of course automatically.

Thanks
Hermann

    geom_point ( aes (x=pos, y=logpval, colour = factor (modd))) + scale_colour_brewer(palette="Set1")+

      scale_x_continuous(breaks = hu, labels = zu)+
        ylim (yd,yh)+
  ylab ("-log10 pval") + xlab ("Chromosomes")+
    ggtitle (title)+
  geom_hline (yintercept = lb, colour = "red")+
       geom_text (data = subset (df, pval < bonp), aes ( x=pos, y=logpval, label =snpid, hjust=0, vjust=0.5))+ #LABEL TERM
    theme_bw()+
      theme(panel.grid.major.x = element_blank())+
        theme (legend.position = "none")

Any ideas how this might be avoided?

Adam Loveland

messages.body_plain:
Sorry about that. It is fixed below, or a gist here:  https://gist.github.com/SChamberlain/5800746

#' Make combined histogram/line plot for visualizing logistic regression.
#'
#' @import ggplot2 gridExtra grid
#' @param data
#' @examples
#' loghistplot(mtcars[,c("mpg","vs")])
#' loghistplot(movies[,c("rating","Action")])
loghistplot <- function(data)
{

  names(data) <- c('x','y') # rename columns

  # get min and max axis values
  min_x <- min(data$x)
  max_x <- max(data$x)
  min_y <- min(data$y)
  max_y <- max(data$y)

  # get bin numbers
  bin_no <- max(hist(data$x)$counts) + 5

  # create plots
  a <- ggplot(data, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
    theme_bw(base_size=16) +
    geom_smooth(method = "glm", family = "binomial", se = TRUE,
                colour='black', size=1.5, alpha = 0.3) +
    # scale_y_continuous(limits=c(0,1), breaks=c(0,1)) +
    scale_x_continuous(limits=c(min_x,max_x)) +
    theme(panel.grid.major = element_blank(),
          panel.grid.minor=element_blank(),

          plot.background = element_blank(),
          panel.background = element_rect(fill =  NA),
          panel.border = element_rect(fill=NA)) +

    labs(y = "Probability\n", x = "\nYour X Variable")

  b <- ggplot(data[data$y == unique(data$y)[1], ], aes(x = x)) +
    theme_bw(base_size=16) +
    geom_histogram(fill = "grey") +
    scale_y_continuous(limits=c(0,bin_no)) +
    scale_x_continuous(limits=c(min_x,max_x)) +

    theme(panel.grid.major = element_blank(),panel.grid.minor=element_blank(),
          axis.text.y = element_blank(), axis.text.x = element_blank(),
          axis.ticks = element_blank(),
          panel.border = element_blank(),

          plot.background = element_blank(),
          panel.background = element_rect(fill =  NA),
          panel.border = element_rect(fill=NA)) +

    labs(y='\n', x='\n')

  c <- ggplot(data[data$y == unique(data$y)[2], ], aes(x = x)) +
    theme_bw(base_size=16) +
    geom_histogram(fill = "grey") +
    scale_y_continuous(trans='reverse', limits=c(bin_no,0)) +
    scale_x_continuous(limits=c(min_x,max_x)) +
    theme(panel.grid.major = element_blank(),panel.grid.minor=element_blank(),
          axis.text.y = element_blank(), axis.text.x = element_blank(),
          axis.ticks = element_blank(),
          panel.border = element_blank(),

          plot.background = element_blank(),
          panel.background = element_rect(fill =  NA),
          panel.border = element_rect(fill=NA)) +

    labs(y='\n', x='\n')

  grid.newpage()
  pushViewport(viewport(layout = grid.layout(1,1)))

  vpa_ <- viewport(width = 1, height = 1, x = 0.5, y = 0.5)
  vpb_ <- viewport(width = 1, height = 1, x = 0.5, y = 0.5)
  vpc_ <- viewport(width = 1, height = 1, x = 0.5, y = 0.5)

  # these three used to lay on top of one another, no
  print(b, vp = vpc_)
  print(c, vp = vpa_)
  print(a, vp = vpb_)

}

messages.subject: Re: Plotting Histograms and a Logistic Curve on the Same Plot
messages.subject_clean: Plotting Histograms and a Logistic Curve on the Same Plot
messages.body_plain:
Thanks Scott.

I actually attempted to build the same type of plot a different way. I plot a logistic regression curve, and then I manually add histograms using geom_bar. So this is all one ggplot object, instead of 3 plots overlain. To create the histograms, I used hist to do the binning, and then scaled them to fit the scale of the logistic plot. It may be a little slow if you have lots of data because it creates the plot twice: once to get the scale and once for the final plot. I also included a non-linear spline fit because that is the type of thing I like to look at.

I also wrote it so it returns a ggplot object that you can add more layers to.

Here is the function (http://gist.github.com/andland/5806238):

logithistplot <- function(data,breaks="Sturges",se=TRUE) {
    require(ggplot2);
    col_names=names(data)

    # get min and max axis values

    min_x <- min(data[,1])
    max_x <- max(data[,1])

    # get bin numbers
    hist_both <- hist(data[,1],plot=FALSE,breaks=breaks)
    hist0 <- hist(data[data[,2]==0,1],breaks=hist_both$breaks,plot=FALSE)
    hist1 <- hist(data[data[,2]==1,1],breaks=hist_both$breaks,plot=FALSE)
    max_count=max(c(hist0$counts,hist1$counts))

    # create plots
    a <- ggplot(data, aes_string(x = col_names[1], y = col_names[2])) +
      theme_bw(base_size=16) +
      geom_smooth(method = "gam", family = "binomial", se = se,
                  aes(colour='Spline',fill='Spline'), size=1.5,formula=y~s(x,bs="cr"))+
      geom_smooth(method = "glm", family = "binomial", se = se,
                  aes(colour='Logit',fill='Logit'), size=1.5) +

      # scale_y_continuous(limits=c(0,1), breaks=c(0,1)) +
      scale_x_continuous(limits=c(min_x,max_x)) +
      theme(panel.grid.major = element_blank(),
            panel.grid.minor=element_blank(),

            panel.background = element_blank()) +
      guides(fill=FALSE)+
      labs(y = "Probability\n", x = paste0("\n",col_names[1]), colour="Method")

    y_range_orig=ggplot_build(a)$panel$ranges[[1]]$y.range
    y_range=y_range_orig
    if (y_range[1]<0) y_range[1]=0
    if (y_range[2]>1) y_range[2]=1
    min_y <- min(y_range[1])
    max_y <- max(y_range[2])

    # need blank bar up to y_min, bars for 0's, blank bars up to 1's, bars for 1's up to y_max
    hist_df=data.frame(mids=hist_both$mids,
                       counts_below=min_y,
                       counts0=hist0$counts/max_count*diff(y_range)/2,
                       counts_mid=diff(y_range)-hist_both$counts/max_count*diff(y_range)/2,
                       counts1=hist1$counts/max_count*diff(y_range)/2)
    hist.m=melt(hist_df,id=1)
    head(hist.m)
    ggplot()+geom_bar(data=hist.m,aes(mids,value,fill=variable),stat="identity")+coord_cartesian(ylim=y_range)+scale_fill_manual(values=c(NA, "grey", NA,"grey"))+guides(fill=FALSE)

    (a <- ggplot(data, aes_string(x = col_names[1], y = col_names[2])) +
      theme_bw(base_size=16) +
      geom_bar(data=hist.m,aes(mids,value,fill=variable),stat="identity")+
      coord_cartesian(ylim=y_range_orig)+
      scale_fill_manual(values=c(NA,NA,"grey","grey","red","blue"))+
      geom_smooth(method = "gam", family = "binomial", se = se,
                  aes(colour='Spline',fill='Spline'), size=1.5,formula=y~s(x,bs="cr"))+
      geom_smooth(method = "glm", family = "binomial", se = se,
                  aes(colour='Logit',fill='Logit'), size=1.5) +
      guides(fill=FALSE)+
      labs(y = "Probability\n", x = paste0("\n",col_names[1]), colour="Method"))
    a
}

messages.body_plain:
theme_grey() and theme_bw() are theme functions that control the
non-data aspects of a ggplot. The background color is a theme
*element*, whose values can be set to constants. My guess is that you
probably want something like geom_rect() here; please provide a
suitable reproducible example so that someone can give you a tangible
answer. At the moment, my answer would be probably yes, but not the
way you think.

Dennis

messages.subject: Re: multiple lines plots with different colours
messages.subject_clean: multiple lines plots with different colours
messages.body_plain:
To separate colors between Barcelona and the other provinces, you need to create an indicator variable for Barcelona. Since you want different colors by age and Barcelona/not Barcelona combinations, the interaction() function can be used. I think the following code does the core of what you asked for, albeit rather crudely. I also thought it would be better to plot the province names rather than the geoorder, so there are a few lines for that purpose.

# Pick out the unique province names and corresponding geoorders,
# then reorder the province names by geoorder
x <- unique(DFsel$prov_name)
y <- unique(DFsel$prov_geoorder)
z <- x[y]

DFsel$age_TFR <- factor(DFsel$age_TFR)
DFsel$order <- factor(DFsel$order, levels = c(1, 2, 11))
DFsel$province <- factor(DFsel$prov_name, levels = z)

# Restrict to order = 11 observations
DFsel11 <- subset(DFsel, order == 11)

# Create the Barcelona indicator and interact it with age_TFR
# The names I chose are ugly - hopefully you can do better.
DFsel11$barca <- DFsel11$prov_name == "Barcelona"
DFsel11$barcage <- with(DFsel11, interaction(barca, age_TFR))
DFsel11$barcage <- factor(DFsel11$barcage, labels = c("~Barcelona1",
                           " Barcelona1", "~Barcelona2", " Barcelona2"))

ggplot(DFsel11, aes(year, value, colour = barcage)) +
     geom_line(size = 1) +
     scale_colour_manual(values = c("orange", "firebrick", "blue", "black")) +
     scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(1980, 2000)) +
     labs(x = NULL, y = "", colour = "ageTFR") +
     facet_wrap(~ province, ncol=6) +
     ggtitle("Total Period Fertility Rate: Age contribution to total fertility") +

     theme(axis.text    = element_text(colour="grey", size=8, angle=0,
                                      face = "plain"),
           axis.text.x  = element_text(hjust=.5, vjust=.7),
           axis.text.y  = element_text(hjust=1, vjust=0),
           strip.text.x = element_text(size = 8, colour =
                                        "black", angle = 0),

           plot.title   = element_text(size = 16),

           plot.margin  = unit(c(1,1,1,1), "cm")
          )

You may want to consider putting the legend at the bottom (legend.position = "bottom" in theme()) to provide a bit more horizontal space for the panels.

Dennis

Looking at those graphs, I doubt they were made with ggplot2. There are
two things about Figure 3 in particular that would be difficult to do:
the y axis is repeated on the right side, not just the left and some of
the fills use patterns (hatching), not just colors. Both of these could
easily be done in a post-processing step with an image manipulation
program, however.

The graph seems to be a pair of ecdf functions, one with the x-axis
mirrored. The vertical breaks are based on the data and could be
pre-computed.

messages.subject: Avoiding extra call to lm()
messages.body_plain:
I was recently asked how to modify the legend text of a plot with several best fit lines
(using lm() ) so that the R2 gets added to the legend text for each year.

The data.frame is of the form
df=data.frame(days=days,x=xvals,y=yvals)

and the plot commands are:
p1 = ggplot(df,aes(x,y,color=as.factor(year(days))))+geom_point()
p2 = p1 + geom_smooth(method="lm",se=FALSE)

My solution was to calculate the lm() again and create a new text label for the scale

r2s=ddply(df,.(year(days)),summarise, r2=format(summary(lm(y~x))$r.squared,digits=3))
r2s$texti=paste(r2s[,1]," (",r2s$r2,")",sep="")
p3 = p2+scale_color_discrete(labels=r2s$texti,name="Year (R2)")

Now, this works. However, calling lm() again annoys me. Is there a way to
get the results from the lm call within geom_smooth(method="lm") instead
of repeating the lm call ?

Halldor

ps. example with made up data attached.

messages.body_plain:
I've a data frame (mmt.ranking.sum_2, attached) with a list of 25 questions (1st column).
The questions are consecutively indexed: 9a-h, 10a-j, 11a-g as part of the question string.
For each question there are counts of answers in classes from 0-5 (2.-7. column), which should be stacked

aaa<-melt(mmt.ranking.sum_2[,1:7], id.vars="questions")
ggplot(aaa,aes(questions, value, fill=variable)) + geom_bar()+ coord_flip() + theme_bw()+ scale_fill_brewer()

In the original data frame & in the melted one the order of the questions is correct 9a-h, 10a-j, 11a-g.
But the order changes & reverses strangely in the final, horizontal chart: 9h-9a, 11g-11a, 10j-10a

This has already been answered here:
http://stackoverflow.com/questions/17194798/ggplot-stacked-bar-chart-order-of-x-values-get-mixed-up

with

+ geom_bar(stat='identity')
+ theme_bw()
+ coord_flip()
+ scale_fill_brewer()

The general order now is ok. 9a - 11g
But in the final (horizontal) chart they are listed bottom up instead of top down.

I have moved to this mailing list because I think this behaviour might be specifically caused by the coord_flip() funktion.
Any suggestions how to achieve a top-down vertical order 9a-11g?

Thanks
Georg

messages.body_plain:
Hi:

On Thu, Jun 20, 2013 at 3:31 AM, g.fritsch <g.fr...@boku.ac.at> wrote:
> I've a data frame (mmt.ranking.sum_2, attached) with a list of 25 questions
> (1st column).
> The questions are consecutively indexed: 9a-h, 10a-j, 11a-g as part of the
> question string.
> For each question there are counts of answers in classes from 0-5 (2.-7.
> column), which should be stacked
>
> aaa<-melt(mmt.ranking.sum_2[,1:7], id.vars="questions")
> ggplot(aaa,aes(questions, value, fill=variable)) + geom_bar()+ coord_flip()
> + theme_bw()+ scale_fill_brewer()
>
> In the original data frame & in the melted one the order of the questions is
> correct 9a-h, 10a-j, 11a-g.
> But the order changes & reverses strangely in the final, horizontal chart:
> 9h-9a, 11g-11a, 10j-10a

It's not strange if you understand the types of objects you're using.
My guess is that the questions variable is a factor, which by default
uses lexicographic ordering. You have to explicitly set the levels of
this factor variable to get the ordering you want. [BTW, this is one
reason why sending data sometimes is not sufficient; whether questions
is a character variable or a factor matters in this case. This is why
the output from the dput() function (whose argument is your R object
of interest) is more informative for potential helpers.]

>
> This has already been answered here:
> http://stackoverflow.com/questions/17194798/ggplot-stacked-bar-chart-order-of-x-values-get-mixed-up

...well, maybe...

>
> with
> ggplot(aaa, aes(reorder(questions,as.numeric(gsub('([0-9]+).*','\\1',
> aaa$questions))) ,value, fill=variable))
> + geom_bar(stat='identity')
> + theme_bw()
> + coord_flip()
> + scale_fill_brewer()
>
> The general order now is ok. 9a - 11g
> But in the final (horizontal) chart they are listed bottom up instead of top
> down.
>
> I have moved to this mailing list because I think this behaviour might be
> specifically caused by the coord_flip() funktion.
> Any suggestions how to achieve a top-down vertical order 9a-11g?

coord_flip() will take the minimum value on the original horizontal
axis and put it on top in the rotated graphic; if you think about it,
that's why the function is called coord_flip. The real problem is the
way that your questions are ordered as a factor. The following is not
especially elegant, but it shows how to define a factor in the aaa
data frame that will order the questions as you want.

# Extract out the question number and part
aaa$q1 <- vapply(aaa$questions,
                 function(x) unlist(strsplit(as.character(x), " "))[1],
                 character(1))
# Extract the unique question names
qlbl <- unique(as.character(aaa$questions))
# Define an ordering vector from 9a-11g
ord <- paste0(rep(9:11, c(8, 10, 7)), c(letters[1:8], letters[1:10],
letters[1:7]))
# Want reverse ordering and labels for the plot
aaa$q <- factor(aaa$q1, levels = rev(ord), labels = rev(qlbl))

ggplot(aaa, aes(x = q, y = value, fill = variable)) +
   geom_bar(stat = "identity") +
   theme_bw() +
   labs(y = NULL) +
   coord_flip() +
   scale_fill_brewer()

If you want to rename the legend title, add fill = "<new-name>" to the
labs() statement.

Dennis

messages.subject: Circular color scale
messages.body_plain:
Hi list,
I'd like to generate an circular continuous color/fill scale to indicate direction (angular data). For instance the gradient would be, North, blue; East, white; South, red; West dark purple (and would loop to blue). That would create a North-south gradient in the blue-red and a light-dark gradient along the East-West axis. The problem with actual gradients is that either colors aren't looping (sharp break between first and last color) or colors are repeated (first and last colors are the same in order for the gradient to loop). That's what happen when I use scale_fill_gradientn(). So my question is two folds how to generate a scale_fill_circular and then add a circular scale to a plot.

Here's a visual explanation :

circular_scale <- function(from = 0, to = 2 * pi, steps = 8, by = to / steps, offset = -pi * by / to, vertical = 3, colours = c("#0088FF", "#ffffff", "#F51D1D", "#400038", "#0088FF"), text_colour = "#aaaaaaaa") {
  pp = data.frame(x = seq(from, to, by = by), y = vertical - 1)
  ggplot(pp, aes(x=x, y=y)) +
    geom_tile(aes(fill = x)) +
    geom_text(aes(label = round(x, 1)), colour = text_colour) +
  list(scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, vertical)),
       scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(from, to, by = by)),
       coord_polar(start = offset) ,
       scale_fill_gradientn(colours = colours, limits = c(from, to)),
}

circular_scale(0, 360)

# As I increase the steps, the problem is less and less obvious :
circular_scale(steps = 40)

This is a mock-up of the result I'd like to achieve (pixel orientation of the volcano dataset).

 <https://lh4.googleusercontent.com/-c-I1jFZDLU4/UcNLGqG-GjI/AAAAAAAAB90/MNASswa6Yog/s1600/aspect.png>

Any help would be appreciated; suggestions of prettier colors would also be welcome.

Etienne

I see it too; it's got to be a bug somewhere.  Here is what I have
figured out about it so far.

It is not a coincidence that the missing segment is the last one in df.
(That appears to be a necessary, but not sufficient, condition).  I can
make this happen with a subset of the data, and it is dependent of the
range of the x-axis.

Using your df and p:

# relevant segment
df[17, ]
##       x xend y
## 17 83.5   83 5
# x range, by default:
range(c(df[1:17, "x"], df[1:17, "xend"]), na.rm = TRUE)
## [1] 24.6 84.5

# segment present
p %+% df[1:17,] + expand_limits(x=10.25) + coord_polar()
# segment absent
p %+% df[1:17,] + expand_limits(x=10.2) + coord_polar()

# segment present
p %+% df[1:17,] + scale_x_continuous(limits=c(10.25, 84.5)) + coord_polar()
# segment absent
p %+% df[1:17,] + scale_x_continuous(limits=c(10.2, 84.5)) + coord_polar()

As you can see, it is very sensitive to what the trained range of x is,
though it does not seem to matter whether it comes from another layer
(via expand_limits) or from the scale itself (via limits argument).

Digging more:

pg <- p %+% df[1:17, ] + scale_x_continuous(limits = c(10.25, 84.5)) +
coord_polar()
pb <- p %+% df[1:17, ] + scale_x_continuous(limits = c(10.2, 84.5)) +
coord_polar()

pgb <- ggplot_build(pg)
pbb <- ggplot_build(pb)

all.equal(pgb, pbb)

relative difference: 0.004878"

1:4, labeled "Unsatisfactory", "Basic", "Proficient" and
"Distinguished". I need to plot stacked bars showing the percentages in

graph. I have managed to do this by plotting the 3 and 4 category
numbers, and then plotting the 1 and 2 multiplied by -1 below the 0
line. But in order to get the order of 1 and 2 to be correct, I had to
switch the percentage values. Here's some of the data:

  scale_y_continuous(name="Percentage", limits=c(-100, 100)) +

I am trying to get bar charts (which I have never done) and I am getting a distorted result.

       Area           type         year   value
1      Andalucia Foreign 2007 1,79125

geom_bar(position="dodge")

what I get is a bar chart with a legend that instead of having three categories (with three different colours) has a legend with shades of blue (as if my category year is continuous). Moreover, the y axis that reports the value has a scale that distorts the interpretation of the graph (instead for instance of having tick marks every 0.1 units it has one at 0.1, 0.05, 0.01 etc).

What I would like instead would be a bar chart with three groups of bars (one group for each year) each group containing two bars ( type variable, one for foreign and one for spanish).

How do I get it?

Thanks for ANY suggestion,

Ale

messages.subject: Alternative similar to geom_density
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I recently created a plot using geom_density and it is really informative about the topic I am studying. However, some of my collaborators worry about the use of density on the y-axis rather than say frequency or raw count because density t is not something that is usually reported in my field. I have spent some time trying to develop a plot using other geom's such as, geom_bar, geom_freqpoly, and geom_area, but really haven't come up with something as nice as the geom_density plot. Nice as in I really like how smooth the overlapping distributions look with geom_density. The others look clunky or jagged. Does anyone have any suggestions on how to make a plot similar to geom_density, but instead of density on the y axis have frequency instead?

Below is some example code to get you started.

date <- abs(round(c(rnorm(n=100,mean=5,sd=1),rnorm(n=50,mean=15,sd=1))))
assign.type <- c(rep("Yes",times=100), rep("No",times=50))
tmp <- data.frame(cbind(date,assign.type))

library(ggplot2)

ggplot(tmp, aes(x=as.numeric(date),fill=assign.type))+
  geom_density(alpha=0.8)

ggplot(tmp, aes(x=as.numeric(date),y=..count..,fill=assign.type, ymax=max(..count..+10)))+
  geom_freqpoly(binwidth=5)

ggplot(tmp, aes(x=as.numeric(date)))+
  geom_area(aes(y = ..count.., fill = assign.type, group = assign.type), stat = "bin",position="dodge")

ggplot(tmp, aes(x=as.numeric(date),fill=assign.type))+
  geom_bar(position="dodge", binwidith=10)

Thanks!
Nick

messages.subject: Re: geom_segment in coord_polar, missing segments
messages.body_plain:
On 6/20/2013 12:42 PM, Brian Diggs wrote:
> On 6/19/2013 5:11 PM, Didac Santesmasses wrote:
>> Hi,
>>
>> I'm trying to plot a tree structure using geom_segment in coord_polar.
>> When the polar coordinates are applied, all the segments are visible.
>> However, when the limits of x axis are modified, some of the segments
>> disappear.
>>
>> Has anyone found anything similar?
>>

[...much example and discussion trimmed...]

I figured out what was the bug was. It had to do with when the final
segment was short enough not to need interpolating to be a curve in
polar coordinates. In that case, the segment was dropped (well, one end
of it was). I've submitted a pull request to fix it:
https://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/pull/823

If you need the fix sooner than when it will be released, you can just
used the modified versions of interp and munch_data in that pull
request, or you can install my branch of it (using devtools):

install_github("ggplot2", "BrianDiggs", ref="fix/munch")

or

install_github("ggplot2", "hadley", pull=823)

--
Brian S. Diggs, PhD
Senior Research Associate, Department of Surgery
Oregon Health & Science University

china_reg2 <- fortify(map("china", fill=FALSE, plot=FALSE))

but just as with map(), you won't be able to properly fill the areas.

HTH,
Ista

This question is going to sound maybe opportunistic, but I am fairly new to R and i would like to know how to plot a single ERP (to start with) using R. I can make basic plots, but if you could show me a script of how time-based signal data can be plotted in R I would be extremely grateful.

My main problem is that I don't know how to make the different conditions appear on the same graph. My idea would be to get data for x(time) in one column of a table and y(amplitudes) on the other, but how can I specify in R another column for y that represents another condition.

Then there is formatting, how to make the graph look more or less like traditional ERP graphs. If you have any script or guidance to offer I would be extremely happy. Thanks B

On Tuesday, January 29, 2013 2:01:40 PM UTC, Sebastian Geukes wrote:
> Hi all,
>
> We have imported EEG data into R to plot event-related potentials using ggplot2. We have obtained beautiful graphs beating out all further attempts using other software. Using facet_wrap() we also manage to plot the ERPs from all of our 32 electrodes at once (see attachment for a rough example).
>
> Now our question is whether there is a neat way in ggplot2 or R base graphics how we could arrange the individual electrode subgraphs such that they approximately reflect the topographical electrode layout on the head? (Just like in the typical ERP top view plots you would get from your dedicated EEG software). Sorting the subgraphs for usage with facet_wrap() obviously won't do the job here.
>
> Is there a way to make up a "plotting canvas" and position the subgraphs to specific coordinates of that canvas? Any other suggestions?
>
> Thank you for any hints!
>
> Sebastian Geukes
> University of Münster, Germany

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I'm trying to draw an overlapped area plot with vertical lines showing the time (x) of the maximum value (y) in each group (two groups).

Right now I just manually draw the lines but I am trying to figure out if there is any function I can use to draw the line based on the max value of each group.  Chang's R graphics cookbook has example adding lines by mean value of each group as follow:

library(plyr) # For the ddply() function
hw_means <- ddply(heightweight, "sex", summarise, heightIn=mean(heightIn))

hw_means
sex heightIn
f 60.52613
m 62.06000

p + geom_hline(aes(yintercept=heightIn, colour=sex), data=hw_means,
linetype="dashed", size=1)

How do I replace the mean function with extracting max value function, if it's possible?

Thank you.
Jinyi

messages.subject: Re: ERP Top View Plot using ggplot2
messages.subject_clean: ERP Top View Plot using ggplot2
messages.body_plain:
I have no idea what an ERP is, but generally, the basic idea in ggplot
is to put all your data into a single (usually) data frame, including
x, y, and any grouping variables. For example, using sample data

d <- data.frame(time=c(1,2,3,1,2,3),condition=c(1,1,1,2,2,2),y=c(1,2,3,4,5,6))

you can do something like

qplot(time,y,color=condition,data=d,geom="line")

to plot the two conditions in different colors.

Ben

This is a little confusing. If you just want the max, use

hw_maxes <- ddply(heightweight, "sex", summarise, heightIn=max(heightIn))

But if you want "the time (x) of the maximum value (y) in each group
(two groups)" then you'll probably want to use the which.max()
function. If you have a sample data set, I or someone else can give a
more concrete answer.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
On Wed, Jun 26, 2013 at 3:34 PM, John Kane <jrkr...@gmail.com> wrote:
> p + scale_x_discrete("My x label") +   # What is this?
>    scale_y_discrete("My y label")

I can confirm that this happens on my system too. It appears to be due to the fact that you are forcing a discrete scale onto integer data.

If you use labs() it doesn't happen because it keeps the scale continuous.

 p+ labs(x="My X Label", y= "My Y Label")

Brandon

messages.subject: Understanding how to format legend title and the number or rows (nrows)
messages.subject_clean: Understanding how to format legend title and the number or rows (nrows)
messages.body_plain:
Hello.
I am having difficulty formatting the legend for a line graph.
I am creating a line graph with five lines plotted over 12 years.  The basic data ("NATDAT")  has this structure:

  REPTYR     VALUE FUEL
1   1999 0.5586435 Coal
2   2000 0.5598068 Coal
3   2001 0.5149410 Coal
4   2002 0.5110911 Coal
5   2003 0.5191403 Coal
6   2004 0.5050716 Coal

where "REPTYR" is on the x-Axis and "VALUE" (in percentages) is on the Y-axis, and lines are differentiated by "FUEL"
The data series repeats five times, with one record per year between 1999 and 2011 for each of five types of fuel.

My call to ggplot2 (version 0.9.3.1) is:

Lines <- c(1,3,4,2,5)  # Line weights
ggplot(NATDAT, aes(x=REPTYR, y=VALUE, linetype = FUEL)) +
  geom_line() +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = Lines) +
  scale_y_continuous("Percentage of Total Annual Generation", limits = c(0,0.65), labels = percent)+
  scale_x_continuous("Year",breaks=c(1999:2011))+
  theme(axis.text.x=element_text(angle=-45, hjust=0), legend.position="bottom") +
   ggtitle ("Total Generation by Fuel Source (%), 1999-2011")

I cannot suppress the title of the legend (which is "FUEL").  I also want to layout the legend in a 2 by 3 arrangement, but I cannot do that either.
I have tried everything I can find on line, but nothing seems to work.
I would appreciate any suggestions you have.

TIA,
AB

BTW, given the power of ggplot2, and the importance of clear legends in publication quality data graphics, I would have thought that controlling the legend would be more straightforward.

messages.subject: Re: Understanding how to format legend title and the number or rows (nrows)
messages.subject_clean: Understanding how to format legend title and the number or rows (nrows)
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
suppressing the legend title is straighforward: simply add: "" as first argument in the scale_linetype_manual command. Controlling the number of columns or rows, you can do with guide=guide_legend(nrow=xx). The numbers of rows or columns depends on the numbers of values you have in the end. The following code should work.

Lines <- c(1,3,4,2,5)  # Line weights
ggplot(NATDAT, aes(x=REPTYR, y=VALUE, linetype = FUEL)) +
  geom_line() +

  scale_linetype_manual("INSERT YOUR TITLE OR LEAVE EMPTY", values = Lines, guide=guide_legend(nrow=2)) +

  scale_y_continuous("Percentage of Total Annual Generation", limits = c(0,0.65), labels = percent)+
  scale_x_continuous("Year",breaks=c(1999:2011))+
  theme(axis.text.x=element_text(angle=-45, hjust=0), legend.position="bottom") +
   ggtitle ("Total Generation by Fuel Source (%), 1999-2011")

Best,
David
